topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Let $a$ and $b$ be positive real numbers. Prove that $\sqrt{ab} \le \frac{a+b}{2}$, and show that equality holds if and only if $a=b$.

solution_steps.title: Non-negativity of Squares
solution_steps.math: (\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0 \quad \forall a, b > 0
solution_steps.explanation: Since every square of a real number is non-negative, $(\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0$.

solution_steps.title: Expansion and Rearrangement
solution_steps.math: (\sqrt{a})^2 - 2\sqrt{a}\sqrt{b} + (\sqrt{b})^2 \ge 0 \implies a - 2\sqrt{ab} + b \ge 0 \implies a + b \ge 2\sqrt{ab}
solution_steps.explanation: Expand the binomial square and move $2\sqrt{ab}$ to the right-hand side.

solution_steps.title: Division by 2
solution_steps.math: \frac{a + b}{2} \ge \sqrt{ab} \iff \sqrt{ab} \le \frac{a+b}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: Dividing both sides by 2 proves the inequality.

solution_steps.title: Condition for Equality
solution_steps.math: \sqrt{ab} = \frac{a+b}{2} \iff (\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b})^2 = 0 \iff \sqrt{a} = \sqrt{b} \iff a = b
solution_steps.explanation: Equality holds if and only if the squared difference is 0, which occurs precisely when $a = b$.

final_answer: $\sqrt{ab} \le \frac{a+b}{2}$, with equality holding if and only if $a = b$.
exam_tip: Do not skip the 'if and only if' biconditional demonstration for the equality case.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: State and prove the Density Theorem for real numbers.
concept_tested: Density Theorem for Rational Numbers in $\mathbb{R}$
approach: Use the Archimedean Property to find an integer denominator $n$ such that $1/n < y - x$, then select the appropriate numerator $m$.

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R} \text{ with } x < y, \; \exists r \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ such that } x < r < y
solution_steps.explanation: Between any two distinct real numbers, there exists at least one rational number.

solution_steps.title: Step 1: Choose Denominator $n$
solution_steps.math: y - x > 0 \implies \exists n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n > \frac{1}{y - x} \iff ny - nx > 1
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ large enough so that the interval $(nx, ny)$ has length strictly greater than 1.

solution_steps.title: Step 2: Choose Numerator $m$
solution_steps.math: \exists m \in \mathbb{Z} \text{ such that } m - 1 \le nx < m
solution_steps.explanation: Every real number $nx$ lies between two consecutive integers. Hence $nx < m$ and $m \le nx + 1$.

solution_steps.title: Step 3: Verification of Bounds
solution_steps.math: nx < m \le nx + 1 < ny \implies nx < m < ny \implies x < \frac{m}{n} < y
solution_steps.explanation: Dividing through by $n > 0$ yields $r = m/n \in \mathbb{Q}$ strictly between $x$ and $y$.

final_answer: The rational number $r = m/n$ satisfies $x < r < y$.
exam_tip: Clearly show how $ny - nx > 1$ ensures an integer $m$ falls strictly inside $(nx, ny)$.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. Prove that (i) $|ab| = |a||b|$, (ii) $|a+b| \le |a| + |b|$.
concept_tested: Properties of Absolute Value: Multiplicative and Subadditive
approach: Prove (i) using sign cases or squaring, and (ii) using $-|a| \le a \le |a|$.

solution_steps.title: Proof of (i) $|ab| = |a||b|$
solution_steps.explanation: Since $|x|^2 = x^2$ for all real numbers and both sides are non-negative, taking the positive square root gives $|ab| = |a||b|$.

solution_steps.title: Proof of (ii) $|a+b| \le |a| + |b|$
solution_steps.math: -|a| \le a \le |a| \quad \text{and} \quad -|b| \le b \le |b|
solution_steps.explanation: By definition of absolute value, $-|x| \le x \le |x|$.

solution_steps.title: Adding Inequalities
solution_steps.math: -(|a| + |b|) \le a + b \le |a| + |b| \iff |a + b| \le |a| + |b|
solution_steps.explanation: Since $-c \le u \le c \iff |u| \le c$, this proves the triangle inequality.

exam_tip: The squaring method for $|ab| = |a||b|$ is much shorter and avoids checking 4 separate sign cases.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ with $x < y$. Prove that there exists an irrational number $z$ such that $x < z < y$.
approach: Scale the interval $(x, y)$ by $1/\sqrt{2}$ and invoke the density of rationals.

solution_steps.title: Transformation by Scaling
solution_steps.math: x < y \implies \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\sqrt{2} > 0$, dividing by $\sqrt{2}$ preserves strict order.

solution_steps.title: Application of Density Theorem
solution_steps.math: \exists r \in \mathbb{Q}, \, r \ne 0 \text{ such that } \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < r < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Density Theorem, between any two reals there is a rational; since $(x/\sqrt{2}, y/\sqrt{2})$ contains infinitely many rationals, choose a non-zero one.

solution_steps.title: Return to Original Variable
solution_steps.math: x < r\sqrt{2} < y, \quad z = r\sqrt{2} \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}
solution_steps.explanation: Multiplying through by $\sqrt{2} > 0$. Since $r \ne 0$ is rational and $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, $z = r\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.

final_answer: $z = r\sqrt{2}$ is an irrational number satisfying $x < z < y$.
exam_tip: Make sure to explicitly mention $r \ne 0$; if $r=0$, $z=0$ which is rational!

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: State and prove the Archimedean Property of $\mathbb{R}$.
approach: State the property and prove it using the Supremum Property (Completeness).

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \; \exists n_x \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n_x > x
solution_steps.explanation: Equivalently: if $y > 0$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $ny > x$.

solution_steps.title: Proof by Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \text{Suppose } \exists x \in \mathbb{R} \text{ s.t. } n \le x \; \forall n \in \mathbb{N}
solution_steps.explanation: Then the set $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded above by $x$. Since $\mathbb{N} \ne \emptyset$ ($1 \in \mathbb{N}$), $\mathbb{N}$ is a non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ bounded above.

solution_steps.title: Existence of Supremum
solution_steps.math: u = \sup \mathbb{N} \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Property of $\mathbb{R}$, the supremum $u$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction via Supremum Characterization
solution_steps.math: u - 1 < u \implies \exists m \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } m > u - 1 \implies m + 1 > u
solution_steps.explanation: Since $m \in \mathbb{N}$, $m + 1 \in \mathbb{N}$. But $m + 1 > u$, contradicting that $u$ is an upper bound of $\mathbb{N}$.

final_answer: Hence $\mathbb{N}$ is unbounded above in $\mathbb{R}$, proving the Archimedean Property.
exam_tip: List the two corollaries often asked: (1) $\inf\{1/n : n \in \mathbb{N}\} = 0$, (2) $\exists n$ with $1/n < \epsilon$ for any $\epsilon > 0$.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: State and prove the Density Theorem for rational numbers in $\mathbb{R}$.
approach: Rigorous full proof with all cases ($x > 0$, $x = 0$, $x < 0$).

solution_steps.title: Statement
solution_steps.math: \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R} \text{ with } x < y, \; \exists q \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ such that } x < q < y
solution_steps.explanation: Between any two distinct real numbers lies a rational number.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: $x > 0$
solution_steps.math: y - x > 0 \implies \exists n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } n(y - x) > 1 \iff ny - nx > 1
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property, such an $n \in \mathbb{N}$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Selecting the Integer $m$
solution_steps.math: A = \{k \in \mathbb{N} : k > nx\} \ne \emptyset \implies m = \min A \implies m - 1 \le nx < m
solution_steps.explanation: By Well-Ordering Principle of $\mathbb{N}$, $A$ has a least element $m$.

solution_steps.title: Establishing the Inequality
solution_steps.math: nx < m \le nx + 1 < ny \implies nx < m < ny \implies x < \frac{m}{n} < y
solution_steps.explanation: Dividing by $n$ produces $q = m/n \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $x < q < y$.

solution_steps.title: General Cases ($x \le 0$)
solution_steps.math: \text{If } x \le 0, \text{ choose } k \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } x + k > 0, \text{ find } q' \in (x+k, y+k), \text{ then } q = q' - k \in (x, y)
solution_steps.explanation: Shifting by an integer $k$ reduces the general case to the positive case.

final_answer: There exists a rational number $q \in (x, y)$ for any $x < y$.
exam_tip: Showing how the case $x \le 0$ reduces to $x > 0$ via integer shift earns full marks.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Let $S$ be a non-empty subset of $\mathbb{R}$ that is bounded below. Prove that $\inf(S) = -\sup(\{-x : x \in S\})$.
approach: Show that $-\sup(-S)$ is a lower bound of $S$ and is greater than or equal to every lower bound.

solution_steps.title: Define $-S$ and verify bounds
solution_steps.math: -S = \{-x : x \in S\}. \quad S \text{ bounded below by } w \implies x \ge w \; \forall x \in S \implies -x \le -w \; \forall -x \in -S
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $-S$ is non-empty and bounded above by $-w$. Hence $u = \sup(-S)$ exists by completeness.

solution_steps.title: Show $-u$ is a lower bound of $S$
solution_steps.math: -x \le u \; \forall x \in S \implies x \ge -u \; \forall x \in S
solution_steps.explanation: Multiplying by $-1$ reverses inequality, so $-u$ is a lower bound of $S$.

solution_steps.title: Show $-u$ is the greatest lower bound
solution_steps.math: t \le x \; \forall x \in S \implies -x \le -t \; \forall -x \in -S \implies u = \sup(-S) \le -t \implies -u \ge t
solution_steps.explanation: If $t$ is any lower bound of $S$, then $-t$ is an upper bound of $-S$, so $u \le -t$, which gives $-u \ge t$.

exam_tip: This duality allows every theorem about suprema to be immediately converted to a theorem about infima.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Prove that if $I_n = [a_n, b_n]$ is a nested sequence of closed bounded intervals, then there exists a point $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$ such that $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}^+$.
approach: Define $S = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ and use $\xi = \sup S$ to prove $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$.

solution_steps.title: Nested Condition
solution_steps.math: I_{n+1} \subseteq I_n \iff a_n \le a_{n+1} \le b_{n+1} \le b_n \quad \forall n \in \mathbb{Z}^+
solution_steps.explanation: The left endpoints $(a_n)$ form an increasing sequence and the right endpoints $(b_n)$ form a decreasing sequence.

solution_steps.title: Every $b_m$ is an Upper Bound for $S = \{a_n\}$
solution_steps.math: \forall n, m \in \mathbb{Z}^+, \quad a_n \le a_{\max(n, m)} \le b_{\max(n, m)} \le b_m \implies a_n \le b_m
solution_steps.explanation: Every right endpoint $b_m$ is greater than or equal to every left endpoint $a_n$.

solution_steps.title: Supremum Existence
solution_steps.math: S = \{a_n : n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\} \ne \emptyset \text{ is bounded above by } b_1 \implies \xi = \sup S \in \mathbb{R} \text{ exists}
solution_steps.explanation: By the Completeness Axiom of $\mathbb{R}$, $\xi = \sup S$ exists.

solution_steps.title: Verification that $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$
solution_steps.math: a_n \le \xi \; \forall n \quad \text{and} \quad \xi \le b_n \; \forall n \implies a_n \le \xi \le b_n \iff \xi \in [a_n, b_n] = I_n
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\xi = \sup S$, $a_n \le \xi$. Since each $b_n$ is an upper bound of $S$, $\xi \le b_n$. Thus $\xi \in I_n$ for all $n$.

final_answer: $\xi = \sup\{a_n : n \in \mathbb{Z}^+\} \in \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty I_n$, so the intersection is non-empty.
exam_tip: If the problem also asks for uniqueness, note that $\inf\{b_n - a_n\} = 0 \implies \xi$ is unique.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Prove that if $x$ and $y$ are real numbers with $x < y$, then there exists an irrational number $z$ such that $x < z < y$.
approach: Use the existence of rationals in $(x/\sqrt{2}, y/\sqrt{2})$.

solution_steps.title: Scale by $\sqrt{2}$
solution_steps.math: x < y \implies \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: Since $\sqrt{2} > 0$, order is preserved.

solution_steps.title: Find Non-zero Rational
solution_steps.math: \exists r \in \mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\} \text{ such that } \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < r < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}}
solution_steps.explanation: Density of rationals provides a non-zero rational $r$ in this open interval.

solution_steps.title: Form Irrational Number
solution_steps.math: z = r\sqrt{2} \implies x < z < y, \quad z \notin \mathbb{Q}
solution_steps.explanation: Product of a non-zero rational and an irrational is irrational.

final_answer: $z = r\sqrt{2}$ is irrational and satisfies $x < z < y$.
exam_tip: Alternatively, you can use $z = x + \frac{y-x}{\sqrt{2} + n}$ for sufficiently large $n$.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Prove the triangle inequality: $|x+y| \le |x| + |y|$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.
approach: Use algebraic properties of absolute values and $-|x| \le x \le |x|$.

solution_steps.title: Inequalities for components
solution_steps.math: -|x| \le x \le |x| \quad \text{and} \quad -|y| \le y \le |y|
solution_steps.explanation: Valid for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$ by definition of $|\cdot|$.

solution_steps.title: Adding inequalities
solution_steps.explanation: Summing the two inequalities maintains the order.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion via Lemma
solution_steps.math: -c \le u \le c \iff |u| \le c \implies |x + y| \le |x| + |y|
solution_steps.explanation: Applying the lemma with $c = |x| + |y|$ and $u = x+y$ completes the proof.

exam_tip: Mention the corollary: $||x| - |y|| \le |x - y|$ (Reverse Triangle Inequality).

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Show that the set of real numbers has no upper bound.
approach: Proof using the Archimedean Property or contradiction via Supremum Property.

solution_steps.title: Definition of Bounded Above
solution_steps.math: \mathbb{R} \text{ is bounded above } \iff \exists M \in \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } x \le M \; \forall x \in \mathbb{R}
solution_steps.explanation: An upper bound must exceed every single real number.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction
solution_steps.math: \text{Take } x_0 = M + 1 \in \mathbb{R}. \quad x_0 = M + 1 > M
solution_steps.explanation: Since $1 > 0$, $M + 1 > M$. But $M + 1 \in \mathbb{R}$, which contradicts that $x \le M$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$.

solution_steps.title: Alternative via Archimedean Property
solution_steps.math: \forall M \in \mathbb{R}, \; \exists n \in \mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{R} \text{ such that } n > M
solution_steps.explanation: Since natural numbers are unbounded above in $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{R}$ itself cannot be bounded above.

final_answer: The set of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ has no upper bound.
exam_tip: The simple element $M+1$ immediately refutes any candidate upper bound $M$.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Let $A$ and $B$ be bounded subsets of $\mathbb{R}$. Prove that $\sup(A + B) = \sup(A) + \sup(B)$ where $A + B = \{a+b : a \in A, b \in B\}$.
concept_tested: Supremum of Sum of Sets: $\sup(A + B) = \sup(A) + \sup(B)$
approach: Show that $\sup A + \sup B$ is an upper bound, and then show that for every $\epsilon > 0$, an element exceeds $\sup A + \sup B - \epsilon$.

solution_steps.title: Step 1: Upper Bound Property
solution_steps.math: a \le \sup A \; (\forall a \in A), \quad b \le \sup B \; (\forall b \in B) \implies a + b \le \sup A + \sup B \; (\forall a+b \in A+B)
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $\sup A + \sup B$ is an upper bound of $A+B$, so $\sup(A+B) \le \sup A + \sup B$.

solution_steps.title: Step 2: Least Upper Bound Property
solution_steps.math: \forall \epsilon > 0, \; \exists a_\epsilon \in A \text{ s.t. } a_\epsilon > \sup A - \frac{\epsilon}{2}, \quad \exists b_\epsilon \in B \text{ s.t. } b_\epsilon > \sup B - \frac{\epsilon}{2}
solution_steps.explanation: By the $\epsilon$-characterization of the supremum for sets $A$ and $B$.

solution_steps.title: Summing Elements
solution_steps.math: a_\epsilon + b_\epsilon \in A + B, \quad a_\epsilon + b_\epsilon > (\sup A + \sup B) - \epsilon
solution_steps.explanation: This shows no number smaller than $\sup A + \sup B$ can be an upper bound of $A+B$.

solution_steps.title: Conclusion
solution_steps.math: \sup(A+B) \ge \sup A + \sup B \implies \sup(A + B) = \sup A + \sup B
solution_steps.explanation: Combining the two inequalities gives exact equality.

exam_tip: Splitting $\epsilon$ into $\epsilon/2 + \epsilon/2$ is the standard technique here.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Show that the set $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 3\}$ has no supremum in $\mathbb{Q}$.
approach: Show that the least upper bound of $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 3\}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is $\sqrt{3}$, which is not rational.

solution_steps.title: Properties of $S$
solution_steps.math: S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 3\} \subset \mathbb{Q}. \quad 1 \in S \implies S \ne \emptyset; \quad x < 2 \; \forall x \in S
solution_steps.explanation: $S$ is non-empty and bounded above in $\mathbb{Q}$ (e.g. by 2).

solution_steps.title: Supremum in $\mathbb{R}$
solution_steps.math: \sup_\mathbb{R}(S) = \sqrt{3}
solution_steps.explanation: In $\mathbb{R}$, $S$ has supremum $\sqrt{3}$.

solution_steps.title: Irrationality of $\sqrt{3}$
solution_steps.math: \sqrt{3} \notin \mathbb{Q}
solution_steps.explanation: If $\sqrt{3} = p/q$ in lowest terms, $p^2 = 3q^2 \implies 3|p \implies 9|p^2 \implies 3|q$, contradicting $\gcd(p, q) = 1$.

solution_steps.title: Non-existence in $\mathbb{Q}$
solution_steps.math: \forall q \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ with } q > 0: \quad q^2 < 3 \implies \exists q' \in S \text{ with } q' > q; \quad q^2 > 3 \implies \exists q'' \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ upper bound with } q'' < q
solution_steps.explanation: Hence no rational number can serve as the least upper bound of $S$ inside $\mathbb{Q}$.

final_answer: The set $S = \{x \in \mathbb{Q} : x^2 < 3\}$ has no supremum in $\mathbb{Q}$.
exam_tip: State clearly that this proves $\mathbb{Q}$ fails the Completeness Axiom.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Prove that if $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a non-empty bounded set, and $c \ge 0$, then $\sup(cS) = c \sup(S)$.
concept_tested: Homogeneity of Supremum for Non-negative Scaling
approach: Consider cases $c = 0$ and $c > 0$, using order preservation of multiplication by positive numbers.

solution_steps.title: Case $c = 0$
solution_steps.math: cS = \{0 \cdot s : s \in S\} = \{0\} \implies \sup(cS) = 0 = 0 \cdot \sup S
solution_steps.explanation: Trivial case when $c = 0$.

solution_steps.title: Case $c > 0$: Upper Bound
solution_steps.math: s \le \sup S \; \forall s \in S \implies cs \le c \sup S \; \forall cs \in cS
solution_steps.explanation: Multiplying by $c > 0$ preserves inequality, so $c \sup S$ is an upper bound of $cS$.

solution_steps.title: Case $c > 0$: Least Upper Bound
solution_steps.math: u \text{ is any upper bound of } cS \implies cs \le u \implies s \le \frac{u}{c} \; \forall s \in S \implies \sup S \le \frac{u}{c} \implies c \sup S \le u
solution_steps.explanation: Since $c > 0$, dividing by $c$ gives $u/c$ as an upper bound of $S$. Therefore $\sup S \le u/c$, so $c \sup S \le u$.

exam_tip: Remember to address the case $c = 0$ separately.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Prove that there does not exist a rational number $r$ such that $r^2 = 2$.
approach: Assume $r = p/q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $\gcd(p, q) = 1$, square both sides and show both $p$ and $q$ must be even.

solution_steps.title: Hypothesis for Contradiction
solution_steps.math: r = \frac{p}{q} \in \mathbb{Q}, \quad p, q \in \mathbb{Z}, \, q \ne 0, \, \gcd(p, q) = 1, \quad r^2 = 2
solution_steps.explanation: Assume $r$ is rational in lowest terms.

solution_steps.title: Parity of $p$
solution_steps.math: \frac{p^2}{q^2} = 2 \implies p^2 = 2q^2 \implies p^2 \text{ is even} \implies p \text{ is even}
solution_steps.explanation: The square of an odd number $(2k+1)^2 = 4k^2+4k+1$ is odd. Thus $p$ must be even, so $p = 2k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.

solution_steps.title: Parity of $q$
solution_steps.math: (2k)^2 = 2q^2 \implies 4k^2 = 2q^2 \implies q^2 = 2k^2 \implies q^2 \text{ is even} \implies q \text{ is even}
solution_steps.explanation: Thus $q$ must also be even.

solution_steps.title: Contradiction
solution_steps.math: 2 | p \quad \text{and} \quad 2 | q \implies \gcd(p, q) \ge 2
solution_steps.explanation: Contradicts the assumption that $\gcd(p, q) = 1$.

final_answer: There is no rational number $r$ such that $r^2 = 2$.
exam_tip: State clearly the lemma: 'If $p^2$ is even, then $p$ is even'.

topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: Find all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ that satisfy the equation $|x + 1| + |x - 2| = 7$.
approach: Partition $\mathbb{R}$ into intervals determined by critical points $x = -1$ and $x = 2$.

solution_steps.title: Critical Points and Intervals
solution_steps.math: \text{Critical points: } x = -1, \, x = 2. \quad \text{Intervals: } (-\infty, -1), \; [-1, 2], \; (2, \infty)
solution_steps.explanation: The behavior of $|x+1|$ and $|x-2|$ changes at $x = -1$ and $x = 2$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: $x < -1$
solution_steps.math: -(x+1) - (x-2) = 7 \implies -2x + 1 = 7 \implies -2x = 6 \implies x = -3
solution_steps.explanation: Check: $-3 < -1$, so $x = -3$ is a valid solution.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: $-1 \le x \le 2$
solution_steps.math: (x+1) - (x-2) = 7 \implies x + 1 - x + 2 = 7 \implies 3 = 7 \quad (\text{No solution})
solution_steps.explanation: In this interval the sum of distances is constant and equals 3, which cannot equal 7.

solution_steps.title: Case 3: $x > 2$
solution_steps.math: (x+1) + (x-2) = 7 \implies 2x - 1 = 7 \implies 2x = 8 \implies x = 4
solution_steps.explanation: Check: $4 > 2$, so $x = 4$ is a valid solution.

exam_tip: Always verify candidate solutions against the interval condition for that case.
